notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources gathered.

---

# 1 Samuel 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter marks the great transition in Israel from theocracy (God as King, ruling through judges) to monarchy. The elders approach Samuel at Ramah, citing his old age and his sons' corruption, and demand "a king to judge us like all the other nations." Though the request displeases Samuel, God instructs him to heed the people — but first to warn them solemnly about what a human king will do. The people insist, and God grants their wish in what the commentators widely describe as an act of permissive, even punitive, concession.

---

## v. 1 — "When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel."

- **Samuel's age:** Gill notes the Jewish tradition that Samuel was only 52, though some say 60–70. The Pulpit Commentary suggests he was "probably not more than sixty" since he lived many years beyond this, into Saul's reign. MacArthur (cited at Precept Austin) estimates about 60 years of age (1043 B.C.). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)
- **"He made his sons judges":** Wesley clarifies these were not "supreme judges" but deputies, subordinate to Samuel, with right of appeal to him. Gill agrees they were judges "under himself." The Pulpit Commentary says Samuel delegated authority because of "the weight of increasing years." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **A sin on Samuel's part?** Enduring Word (David Guzik) states plainly: "Samuel was one of the godliest men in the entire Bible. Yet his action here may be a sin on his part. We never have the pattern of judges being appointed by men or of the office of judge being passed from father to son." Precept Austin agrees it was "poor judgment" and notes that God's pattern was to raise up judges Himself. Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary adds: "There is nothing said about the Lord instructing Samuel to make his sons judges, so this is likely a serious mistake on his part." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **Yet no censure of Samuel as a father:** Precept Austin notes: "The text does not condemn Samuel for being a poor example or a bad father," unlike Eli who was judged for not restraining his sons (1 Sam 3:13). Garner-Howes adds: "Samuel is not censured by the Lord as was Eli, so the nature of their error is not the same." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 2 — "The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second was Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba."

- **Meaning of the names:** Pulpit Commentary notes both names are "pledges of [Samuel's] faith — Joel meaning Jehovah is God, and Abiah Jab is Father." Precept Austin adds that "having even a godly father in a high office does not qualify his son for a similar office." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)
- **Beersheba:** The Pulpit Commentary locates it "in the extreme south of the tribe of Judah," about 50 miles from Ramah. Samuel's placing them there proves his rule "was acknowledged throughout the whole country." Josephus (Antiquities 6.3.2) states one son was at Bethel and the other at Beersheba, though the Pulpit Commentary doubts this. Precept Austin notes the distance may have contributed to the problem — "out of sight, out of mind." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)
- **Textual note:** 1 Chronicles 6:28 calls the firstborn "Vashni," which the Pulpit Commentary says is "a mistake" — "Vashni" means "and the second," the name Joel having been omitted from that text. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/8.htm)

---

## v. 3 — "But his sons did not walk in his ways; they turned aside toward dishonest gain, accepting bribes and perverting justice."

- **The core sin:** Gill states they "turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment" — the very sins forbidden in Exodus 23:6, 8 and Deuteronomy 16:19. Wesley notes: "Opportunity and temptation discovered that corruption in them which till now was hid from their father." Precept Austin calls it "Judges for sale" — "instead of pursuing justice, they pursued personal gain." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)
- **Comparison with Eli's sons:** Brian Bell (cited at Precept Austin) observes: "Eli's sons yielded to the lust of the flesh; Samuel's sons were lovers of money." Matthew Henry (also at Precept Austin) notes: "It does not appear that Samuel's sons were so profane and vicious as Eli's sons; but they were corrupt judges, they turned aside after lucre." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)
- **Not "like father, like son":** Precept Austin notes their names meant "Jehovah is God" and "My Father is Jehovah," yet they did not live up to those names. "The privilege of judging left the sons open to the pressure to compromise their integrity." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)

---

## v. 4 — "So all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah."

- **A constitutional assembly:** The Pulpit Commentary notes this was "a popular assembly, representing the Israelite nation, and composed probably of the chiefs and heads of fathers' houses" — a body that had existed since Egypt (Exodus 3:16), outlived the monarchy, and "continued down to New Testament times." The demand, though "a sort of revolt," was "made in a constitutional manner" with "all the weight of a formal decision on the part of the representatives of the nation." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/8.htm)
- **"All the elders":** Bible.org (Bob Deffinbaugh) notes that "as the chapter unfolds, it is very clear that all of the people of Israel are behind this movement," not just the elders. The elders were representatives, not acting independently. (https://bible.org/seriespage/give-us-king-1-samuel-81-22)
- **Ramah:** Samuel's home base, where he had built an altar and judged Israel (1 Sam 7:17). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)

---

## v. 5 — "'Look,' they said, 'you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.'"

- **Two stated reasons — one valid, one not:** Enduring Word says rejecting Samuel's corrupt sons was wise, but desiring a king "like all the nations" was wrong. Constable's Notes (Dispensational) make the same point: "The request in itself was not what displeased Samuel and God. It was the reason they wanted a king that was bad." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-8.html)
- **"Like all the nations":** Wesley writes: "But there was not the like reason; because God had separated them from all other nations, and cautioned them against the imitation of their examples, and had taken them into his own immediate care and government; which privilege other nations had not." Gill adds that Israel "had God for their King in a peculiar manner other nations had not, and stood in no need of any other." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **King vs. judge:** Enduring Word explains the distinction: "A judge was a leader raised up by God, usually to meet a specific need in a time of crisis. When the crisis was over usually the judge went back to doing what he did before. A king not only held his office as king as long as he lived, he also passed his throne down to his descendants." Judges didn't establish a "government"; kings created a "standing government with a bureaucracy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)
- **Was a king inherently wrong?** No — Deuteronomy 17:14–20 shows God had made provision for kingship. Enduring Word stresses the problem was timing and motive: "God knew Israel would have a king, but He wanted to give the king in His timing." Constable adds that God's purpose for Israel was to be "different from the nations, superior to them, and a lesson for them (Exodus 19:5-6)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-8.html)
- **Pretext:** Precept Austin calls the sons' corruption "only a pretext because Beersheba was far out on the fringes of the nation, and all that was needed was for the two men to be deposed as judges. There was no need for a king." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)

---

## v. 6 — "But when they said, 'Give us a king to judge us,' their demand was displeasing in the sight of Samuel; so he prayed to the LORD."

- **Why displeased?** Wesley identifies two reasons: (1) "God was hereby dishonoured by that distrust of him, and that ambition, and itch after changes," and (2) "that great misery, which he foresaw the people would hereby bring upon themselves." Gill adds that Samuel was displeased because "they were for changing their form of government, not only to remove it from him, and his sons, but from the Lord himself." The Pulpit Commentary notes they "had determined to have a king without consulting the will of God" and "undervalued their own religious privileges." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/8.htm)
- **Samuel prayed:** Enduring Word calls this "the right thing to do whenever we are displeased. We should never carry such troubles with us." Quoting F.B. Meyer: "Surely it is the mistake of our life, that we carry our burdens instead of handing them over; that we worry instead of trusting; that we pray so little." Josephus (cited by Gill) says Samuel was so distressed he "could neither eat nor sleep, but watched all night, and spent it in prayer." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 7 — "And the LORD said to Samuel, 'Listen to the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king.'"

- **The heart of the matter:** All commentators agree this verse is the theological centre of the chapter. Gill writes that God "assented to their request" but "it was in anger," citing Hosea 13:11 ("I gave you a king in My anger"). Wesley concurs: "God grants their desire in anger, and for their punishment." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html)
- **"They have not rejected you":** Enduring Word sees God comforting Samuel: "Samuel, don't take it personally. They are not rejecting you, but Me." Gill argues for an absolute (not comparative) reading: "they had not rejected Samuel from all share in the government," since Samuel continued judging all his life, "but they entirely rejected the sole and peculiar government of God over them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **Rejection of theocracy:** The Pulpit Commentary says the nation's real need was "not a new power, but the permanent organisation of what up to this time had been a casual authority." Constable adds that the request "expressed dissatisfaction with God's present method of providing leadership through judges." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/8.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-8.html)
- **Prophetic foreshadowing:** Enduring Word notes that "when Jesus stood before Pilate the Jewish mob declared, 'We have no king but Caesar' (John 19:15). Jesus was a rejected King." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)

---

## v. 8 — "Just as they have done from the day I brought them up out of Egypt until this day, forsaking Me and serving other gods, so they are doing to you."

- **Israel's consistent pattern:** Gill says this was "no new thing" — from the Exodus onward it had been "one continued series of ingratitude, of rebellion against God, and against his servants." Wesley notes God speaks this "for Samuel's comfort and vindication" — "'Thou farest no worse than myself.'" Enduring Word adds: "When the elders of Israel asked for a king, they thought that better politics or government could meet their needs. But if they had just been faithful to their King in heaven, they would not need a king on earth." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)
- **God's patience:** The Pulpit Commentary's homiletical section underscores that God has endured this pattern for centuries, demonstrating His long-suffering. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/8.htm)

---

## v. 9 — "'Now listen to them, but you must solemnly warn them and show them the manner of the king who will reign over them.'"

- **"Manner" (Hebrew *mishpat*):** Gill explains this term means not a divine law or legitimate right, but the "assumed, arbitrary, and despotic power" that kings of the East exercised — "a custom he would introduce." Wesley says: "That, if it be possible, thou mayst yet prevent their sin and misery." Enduring Word calls it an act of making "an informed choice" — "Information creates responsibility." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)
- **Forewarning:** Enduring Word says the goal is not to change their minds (Israel won't), but "to simply forewarn them" so their accountability is increased. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)

---

## v. 10 — "So Samuel spoke all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking him for a king."

- **Faithful transmission:** Gill notes Samuel told them "all the words of the LORD" — including that their request was a rejection of God, that it was consistent with their historic pattern, and that it would be granted but with consequences. Bible.org observes that though Samuel told them "all the words of the LORD," what the text preserves and emphasises is the warning in vv. 11–18 — "the emphasis here in chapter 8 is not the evil of Israel's rejection of God" but "the high cost of a king." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://bible.org/seriespage/give-us-king-1-samuel-81-22)

---

## v. 11 — "He will take your sons and appoint them to his own chariots and horses, to run in front of his chariots."

- **"He will take":** The repeated verb dominates vv. 11–17. Enduring Word notes "Most kings are takers, not givers and they come to be served, not to serve." Wesley adds "Injuriously and by violence." Garner-Howes comments that the draft would break up home life. Constable cites Youngblood: "By nature royalty is parasitic rather than giving, and kings are never satisfied with the worst." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-8.html)
- **Chariots and horses:** Gill notes these were "mean and servile" employments — "what they should be obliged to, whether they would or no." Running before chariots was the work of "running footmen, being swift of foot," citing 2 Samuel 15:1 where Absalom had fifty such men. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 12 — "He will appoint some for himself as commanders of thousands and of fifties, and others to plow his ground, to reap his harvest, to make his weapons of war, and to equip his chariots."

- **Military conscription and forced labour:** Wesley notes these appointments are made "for his own fancy, or glory, and not only when the necessities of the kingdom require it." Even the honour of military rank "was accompanied with great dangers, and pernicious snares" and the public bore the cost. Garner-Howes observes: "The older and more experienced men would be taken from their lands and put to labor on the fields, orchards, vineyards which he would take from their possession." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **"Ear his ground":** Gill explains the archaic English "ear" means "to plough." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 13 — "And he will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers."

- **A particular grief:** Wesley notes taking daughters "would be more grievous to their parents, and more dangerous to themselves, because of the tenderness of that sex, and their liableness to many injuries." Gill comments that these tasks (perfumers/confectioners, cooks, bakers) were "the business of women in those times and places" in the East. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 14 — "He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive groves and give them to his servants."

- **Land confiscation:** Wesley compares this to Ahab and Naboth's vineyard — "by fraud or force." Gill clarifies that kings did not typically seize land outright (otherwise Ahab would not have needed Jezebel's scheme), but rather took the produce — "the fruits of their fields, vineyards, and oliveyards." The Pulpit Commentary sees this as a prophecy that "the king would use his military power to steal the best of their land to give it to his favorite bureaucrats." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)

---

## v. 15 — "He will take a tenth of your grain and grape harvest and give it to his officials and servants."

- **A royal tithe:** Wesley notes this is "besides the several tenths which God hath reserved for his service" — a double tithe. Precept Austin calls this "a pregnant prophecy, for it meant that the king would put himself in the place of God, receiving the tithe." Gill adds that kings of other nations (citing Aristotle on Babylon and Diodorus Siculus on Arabia) regularly collected a tenth, so the Israelites "must expect that they would insist upon the privileges and revenues that others had." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **"Officers"** — Wesley notes the Hebrew literally reads "to his eunuchs," implying the king "should against the command of God, make some of his people eunuchs." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 16 — "And he will take your menservants and maidservants and your best cattle and donkeys and put them to his own use."

- **Confiscation of labour and livestock:** Wesley says "by constraint, and without sufficient recompense." Gill notes the "goodliest young men" were those "tall and lusty, comely and beautiful, of a proper stature and good aspect" — prized for royal service. Garner-Howes emphasises that "the king would not take the young people least desirable, but would choose the best." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 17 — "He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you yourselves will become his slaves."

- **"You yourselves will become his slaves":** Gill records that some (like Abarbinel) interpret this as being made literal slaves "even as the Canaanitish servants were," while others see it more mildly as "being obliged to pay tribute and taxes, for the support of his government." Wesley reads it as: "he will use you like slaves, and deprive you of that liberty which now you enjoy." Precept Austin sees it as a warning that "the people would find themselves in a new Egypt — one of their own choosing." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)

---

## v. 18 — "When that day comes, you will beg for relief from the king you have chosen, but the LORD will not answer you on that day."

- **"Cry out":** Wesley says "Ye shall bitterly mourn for the sad effects of this inordinate desire of a king." Gill emphasises: "they brought all this upon themselves." Garner-Howes adds: "The most terrifying thing about the whole matter is that when the people realized their mistake and wanted relief from the despotism of the king the Lord would turn a deaf ear. It is not that the Lord would no longer bless them when they had got a king, but His meaning is that He would not heed their cry to remove their king. Once they had made to themselves a king there would be no undoing their deed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **"The king you have chosen":** Enduring Word notes the pointed wording: "God will call this coming king your king… If Israel waited for God's king, they would not need to cry out." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)

---

## v. 19 — "Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to Samuel. 'No!' they said. 'We must have a king over us.'"

- **Deliberate refusal:** Gill notes they "refused to obey the voice of Samuel" even though "they knew Samuel was a prophet, and spoke by a spirit of prophecy, and none of his words had ever fallen to the ground." Their obstinacy was wilful. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)
- **The tragedy of insisting on one's own way:** Enduring Word and Precept Austin both stress that God sometimes permits His people to have what they demand, even when it is second-best, so they learn through its consequences. Paul Apple (quoted at Precept Austin): "God's People Have A Tragic History Of Rejecting God's Leadership Model For A Pragmatic, Worldly Model Of Their Own Choosing." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)

---

## v. 20 — "Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles."

- **"Like all the nations" — the fatal refrain:** Wesley exclaims: "What stupidity! It was their happiness that they were unlike all other nations (Numbers 23:9, Deuteronomy 33:28)… But they will have a king to go out before them, and to fight their battles. Could they desire a battle better fought for them than the last was, by Samuel's prayers and God's thunders?" Enduring Word adds that "God just won a spectacular battle for Israel in 1 Samuel 7. Israel did not lack a king — they had a king in the LORD God. What they wanted was the image of a king." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)
- **"Go out before us and fight our battles":** Wesley's grim observation: "Their first king was slain in battle: and so was Josiah, one of the last and best." Garner-Howes adds: "it is very remarkable, and what is observed by some, that their first king died in a battle." Gill connects the timing to the threat from Nahash king of Ammon (1 Sam 12:12), which made them especially eager for a military king. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 21 — "Samuel listened to all the words of the people and repeated them in the hearing of the LORD."

- **Samuel's prayer:** Gill says Samuel "patiently, and without interruption; attentively heard them, took notice of them, laid them up in his memory; but gave no answer to them, but reported them to the Lord." Wesley says he "repeated them privately between God and himself; for his own vindication and comfort: and as a foundation for his prayers to God, for direction and assistance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## v. 22 — "'Listen to their voice,' the LORD said to Samuel. 'Appoint a king for them.' Then Samuel told the men of Israel, 'Everyone must go back to his city.'"

- **God's final permission:** Enduring Word calls this "almost funny. Israel rejected the rule of God, yet they could not escape it, because God appointed their king. God will never step off His throne, even if man asks Him to." Precept Austin labels this section "The Sovereign Permissiveness of Yahweh." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-8-commentary)
- **"Go every man to his city":** Gill says this meant "they might return in peace, and be assured their request would be granted." Bible.org notes: "not knowing who this king will be, Samuel sends the Israelites to their homes until the time when God will indicate the identity of their new king." The search for Saul begins in chapter 9. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://bible.org/seriespage/give-us-king-1-samuel-81-22)
- **"Their king" vs. "His king":** Enduring Word offers a key insight: "God will give Israel 'their king' – Saul. Later, after 'their king' fails, God will give Israel 'His king' – David." If Israel had not been impatient, "God would have made David the first human king of Israel." This is echoed by Constable, who calls Saul a "'false start' to the monarchy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-8.html)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### Reformed / Presbyterian
- **Emphasis on theocracy and God's sovereignty:** The Reformed reading (reflected in Ligonier-linked resources and Constable) stresses that Israel's sin was rejecting God's direct rule. God's sovereignty is never set aside — He permits the monarchy but remains King. Constable: "In spite of His people's rejection, the Lord continued to show them mercy and faithfulness." The request is seen as "one more instance of apostasy." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-8.html)

### Baptist (Particularly as seen in Gill, Spurgeon-tradition, Garner-Howes)
- **Stress on divine permission as judgment:** Gill repeatedly says God assented "in anger" (citing Hosea 13:11). Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary draws explicit lessons about the "permissive will" of God: "the Lord often lets His children have their desires to show them His way is best." There is also a strong warning that "When God's people begin trying to be like the world they will eventually produce a people who do not want the Lord." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-8.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-8.html)

### Methodist / Wesleyan (John Wesley's Notes)
- **Pastoral and practical emphasis:** Wesley focuses on the moral and practical consequences. He highlights the folly of desiring to be "like the nations" when Israel's distinctiveness was their privilege. He also notes that Samuel was "not supposed to have been above sixty" and that age had "cut his hair" — a practical, almost tender observation. Wesley is more willing than some to call Samuel's appointment of sons a reasonable delegation rather than a sin. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-samuel-8.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)
- **Christological typology:** Guzik draws direct contrasts between earthly kings who "take" and Jesus the King of Kings who "came to serve, not to be served" (Matthew 20:28). He also sees a prophetic parallel between Israel's rejection of God as King and the mob's cry "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:15). The application is strongly devotional — "When we're tempted to follow the world's pattern instead of trusting God's plan, we should remember that resisting God's rule only hurts ourselves." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-8/)

### Anglican (Pulpit Commentary / Ellicott)
- **Historical and constitutional interest:** The Pulpit Commentary is distinctive in tracing the "elders" as a constitutional body with continuity from Egypt through to the New Testament Sanhedrin. It also defends Samuel's character warmly: "His conduct in this trying conjuncture was most admirable, and few commentators have done justice to the man, who, possessed of what was virtually kingly power, yet gave it over for the nation's good into the hands of another." Ellicott warns against seeing the monarchy merely as "a vain-glorious popular demand" — there was a providential purpose. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/8.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/8.htm)
